For a **1,000Wh** power station, plan on **about 300–350W of panels to refill it in one sunny day**, or **about 200W if 1.5–2 days is acceptable**. In winter you'd need much more.

## The formula

**Panel watts ≈ battery Wh ÷ (peak sun hours × 0.70–0.75)**

The 0.70–0.75 factor accounts for heat, panel angle, haze, and charge-controller losses. Panels rarely deliver their rated watts outdoors. ([Enough Watts](https://enoughwatts.com/guides/how-much-solar-to-recharge), [Watt48](https://www.watt48.com/guides/solar-panel-charging-power-station))

"Peak sun hours" means the day's sunlight counted as hours of full-strength noon sun. It's not the same as daylight hours. A typical US day gets about 4.5. ([Power Preflight](https://powerpreflight.com/guides/solar-panel-sizing-portable-power-stations/))

## Panel size for a full refill from empty in one day

| Sun conditions | Peak sun hours | Panel watts needed |
|---|---|---|
| Strong summer / Southwest | 6 | ~230W |
| Good summer | 5 | ~270–300W |
| Average US day | 4 | ~340W |
| Mediocre / shoulder season | 3 | ~450W |
| Northern winter | 2 | ~700W+ |

Sources: [power-runtime](https://power-runtime.pages.dev/guides/solar-charging/), [Held in Reserve](https://www.heldinreserve.com/power/solar-panels-recharge-power-station/)

A handy rule of thumb is to divide the battery's Wh by 5. That gives about 200W, which refills 1,000Wh in roughly 1.5 days of average sun (about 630Wh per day). ([Power Preflight](https://powerpreflight.com/guides/solar-panel-sizing-portable-power-stations/))

## Check your station's specs before buying

1. **Maximum solar input (watts).** If your station caps solar at 200W, a 400W panel won't charge it any faster at noon. Modest oversizing does help, though. A bigger panel reaches the cap earlier in the day and holds it longer in clouds or weak light.
2. **Input voltage range.** The panel's open-circuit voltage (Voc) must stay inside the station's limit. Going over can damage the charge controller, so be strict about this, especially if you wire panels in series.
3. **Connector.** Most panels use MC4 plugs, while stations usually take XT60 or barrel plugs. Make sure you have the right adapter.
4. **Running loads at the same time.** Anything you power while charging, like a fridge, subtracts from what goes into the battery.
